strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis: the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression (Figures 1-2) is a useful diagnostic of why sequential SFT-then-RL can underperform pure RL when fine-tuning instruct models, and this analysis directly motivates the method design.

The proposed CHORD is simple, easy to implement, and well-specified: a dynamically weighted auxiliary SFT loss (global coefficient mu with a decay schedule) combined with a token-wise weighting phi(p)=p(1-p) that down-weights both high- and low-probability tokens, addressing entropy collapse and policy disruption simultaneously.

Comprehensive evaluation across two distinct domains (mathematical reasoning with Qwen2.5-7B and tool-use with LLaMA3.2-3B), with a broad baseline suite (Original, SFT-only variants, SFT+RL, GRPO, LUFFY, SASR), ablations on mu schedules (Figure 7), entropy/reward dynamics (Figures 8-9), response-length analyses (Table 2), and detailed per-category results in the appendix.

The paper distinguishes itself from prior unified SFT+RL work (SRFT, LUFFY, Reift, UFT, BREAD) by targeting the more practical and challenging setting of fine-tuning an already instruction-tuned model with a large policy-expert distribution gap, supported by the base-vs-instruct analysis in Appendix C/Figure 12.
Ablations showing that phi(.) makes the method robust to the choice of mu schedule (Appendix A.3, Figure 10) add practical value and reduce hyperparameter sensitivity.
Implementation details, prompts, and code release support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is a weighted sum of two standard losses plus a simple parabolic token weighting p(1-p). Related ideas already exist (importance-sampling-style reweighting in LUFFY/DFT/iw-SFT, sample-level SFT weighting in SRFT), and the paper provides no theoretical grounding for why p(1-p) is optimal beyond empirical observation and an information-theoretic intuition.

Missing direct empirical comparison with SRFT, which the related-work section itself identifies as the closest unified single-stage method; the comparison set relies on LUFFY (which is also under-trained relative to its original setup, using 20k vs 45k samples), weakening the strength of the 'outperforms existing approaches' claim.

Absolute gains over strong baselines are modest on the key benchmarks (e.g., AIME24 18.2 vs 17.1 for SFT-best+RL; AIME25 17.2 vs 17.9 for CHORD-mu; BFCL Overall 78.5 vs 78.1), and AIME benchmarks contain very few problems, so even avg@32 evaluation leaves room for statistical noise; no significance testing is reported.

The interaction between phi and mu is under-analyzed: since phi(p) has a maximum of 0.25, it implicitly rescales the SFT loss magnitude, and the paper does not disentangle whether gains come from the specific parabolic shape, the effective loss re-weighting, or the dual-control structure; alternative weightings are not ablated.

Scale and scope are limited: only 7B/3B models, a single expert model (DeepSeek-R1), and relatively small SFT sets (5k math, 500 tool-use); it is unclear whether the findings generalize to larger models, other expert data sources, or non-verifiable-reward settings.

Results are reported at the best checkpoint selected on the validation set, which may favor methods with more checkpoints/hyperparameter tuning; the hyperparameter search budget per baseline is not fully disclosed.

The claim that phi enables 'selective absorption' of expert knowledge is supported mainly by qualitative case studies (Appendix D) and response-length trends rather than a direct mechanistic analysis.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written. The empirical analysis of the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression when SFT-ing instruction models on off-policy expert data (Figures 1-2) is a useful and reproducible observation that grounds the method design.

The proposed method is simple, interpretable, and easy to implement: a global loss coefficient with a decay schedule, plus a token-wise weighting phi(p) = p(1-p). The dual-control framing (global vs. token-level influence) is intuitive.

The experimental comparison covers a reasonable set of relevant baselines (SFT-only, RL-only, SFT+RL, LUFFY, SASR) across two task domains (math reasoning and tool-use), with useful ablations on the mu schedule, on removing phi, and on base-vs-instruct models (Appendix C).
The response-length and case-study analyses (Tables 2, Appendix D) provide qualitative evidence that CHORD-phi selectively absorbs expert patterns rather than wholesale imitating them.
The distinction from prior 'ZeroRL' work (training from base models vs. finetuning instruct models with established policies) is a legitimate and practically relevant problem framing.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core contribution amounts to (i) a weighted convex combination of SFT and GRPO losses with a decay schedule, and (ii) a p(1-p) token weighting heuristic. Both ingredients are close to existing ideas: sample-level SFT weighting in SRFT, simple on/off-policy data mixing (SimpleMix), tapered off-policy REINFORCE [38], and entropy-based token weighting [44]. The paper's differentiation from these works is argued mainly through the task setting rather than through methodological novelty.

There is an unaddressed tension in the core design: the stated motivation is that RL alone cannot learn capabilities beyond the base model, and expert data is needed to teach new reasoning paths. Yet phi(p) = p(1-p) assigns near-zero weight precisely to the tokens the model finds most improbable - i.e., the genuinely new knowledge. The paper does not reconcile why down-weighting novel tokens still enables capability gains, or when the method would fail (e.g., expert data that is truly out-of-distribution).

Evaluation results are not fully convincing. The margins over the strongest baseline (SFT-best+RL) are small on the headline benchmarks (+1.0 AIME24, +1.6 AIME25), and no variance across training seeds is reported for the final numbers. The +10.5 point jump on MMLU-Pro for CHORD-phi over GRPO (56.2 vs 45.8) is a large anomaly that is not explained or analyzed, raising concerns about cherry-picked checkpoints or evaluation variance.

Hyperparameters appear task-specific and hand-tuned: the mu decay schedule differs substantially between math (0.9 to 0.05 over 200 steps) and tool-use (0.6 to 0.0 over 20 steps), which weakens the claim of a general, robust framework. The 'robustness to mu' claim is only supported for CHORD-phi in one appendix experiment.

The information-theoretic justification for phi is post-hoc and informal; the 'general principle' for instantiating phi is stated but never tested against alternative weightings (e.g., p^alpha, entropy-based, IS-based), so it is unclear whether the specific parabolic form matters.

Baselines may be under-resourced: LUFFY is trained with 20k samples versus 45k in its original work, and footnote caveats suggest the comparisons are not on equal footing. Comparisons with SRFT - the closest unified single-stage method - are discussed but not empirically included.
Claims of 'significant improvements over baselines' overstate what the evidence shows given the small margins, unexplained MMLU-Pro gap, and single-task-specific tuning.

strengths: The empirical characterization of the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression when applying SFT to an instruct model with established patterns (Figures 1-2) is a clear, well-motivated observation that grounds the method design.

The dual-control design (global coefficient μ with a decay schedule + token-wise weighting φ(·) = p(1-p)) is simple, well-motivated by the entropy analysis in Figure 5, and the paper is transparent that it is one instantiation of a general down-weighting principle rather than claiming theoretical optimality.

Comprehensive evaluation across two distinct settings (math reasoning with Qwen2.5-7B and tool-use with LLaMA3.2-3B) with a good set of baselines including recent methods (LUFFY, SASR), plus thorough ablations on fixed vs. dynamic μ, the role of φ(·), and joint μ-schedule tuning (Appendix A.3).
The response-length and case-study analyses (Tables 2-3, Appendix D) provide convincing qualitative evidence that CHORD-φ selectively absorbs expert patterns rather than wholesale imitation.

The distinction from prior 'ZeroRL' work (training from base models vs. instruct models with established policies) is clearly articulated, including empirical support in Appendix C.1, and the implementation is released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core recipe (mixing an SFT loss into on-policy RL with a schedule) is closely related to SRFT, UFT, Reift, SimpleMix, and tapered off-policy REINFORCE [38], and token-level reweighting of SFT losses resembles DFT and iw-SFT [37, 46]. The combination of a μ schedule with φ(·) = p(1-p) is a straightforward heuristic; notably, the two most related methods (SRFT, Reift) are discussed but not empirically compared in Table 1.

The choice of φ(·) = p(1-p) lacks theoretical grounding and ablation against alternatives (e.g., entropy-based weighting, IS-style ratios, threshold/clipping variants); it is unclear whether this specific form or any down-weighting at the probability extremes is what drives the gains.

Some reported gains are small and potentially within noise: e.g., CHORD-φ vs. CHORD-μ on AIME24 (18.2 vs 18.1) and BFCL (78.5 vs 78.1), and CHORD-μ vs. SFT-best+RL margins of ~1-2 points. No statistical significance testing is provided, and results are reported on the best validation-selected checkpoint, which may favor methods with more checkpoints/hyperparameter tuning.
LUFFY is re-run with a reduced training budget (20k vs. 45k samples) relative to its original setup, which weakens the strength of that comparison despite the footnote acknowledgment.

Evaluation is limited to relatively small models (7B and 3B) and narrow task families (math and single-turn tool-use); generalization of the 'established policy disruption' claim to other domains or larger models remains unverified.

The 'shift-readapt-overfit' phenomenon, while nicely illustrated, is consistent with already-reported findings on SFT-then-RL suboptimality [6, 55], so the analysis contribution is confirmatory more than new.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical analysis of the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression when applying SFT to an instruction-tuned model, which offers useful insight into why the SFT-then-RL paradigm can underperform pure RL.

CHORD is simple, computationally cheap (element-wise token weighting), and well-posed: framing SFT as a dynamically weighted auxiliary objective within on-policy RL, with a global coefficient (μ) plus a token-wise weighting function (ϕ(p)=p(1-p)) that down-weights both near-certain and near-impossible tokens.

Evaluation covers a broad range of settings: math reasoning (AIME24/25, AMC, MMLU-Pro), tool-use (ToolACE/BFCL), a non-verifiable medical task (RaR-Medicine), a weaker policy model (Qwen2.5-3B), an MoE architecture (Phi-mini-MoE), and different expert data sources (DeepSeek-R1 vs Qwen2.5-72B), demonstrating robustness and generality.

Baselines are reasonably comprehensive, including recent unified SFT/RL methods (LUFFY, SASR, SRFT) and a dedicated analysis showing that 'zero-RL' methods designed for base models are suboptimal for instruction-tuned models — a practically relevant distinction.

The paper is honest about limitations (e.g., ϕ(·) is one instantiation of a general principle; adaptive μ requires hyperparameter tuning; fixed μ works fine with ϕ), and there are thorough ablations on μ schedules and ϕ variants (entropy-based, IS clip, focal loss).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest. The core method is a weighted combination of GRPO and SFT losses with a decaying coefficient (closely related to scheduled sampling and interleaved SFT/RL), and ϕ(p)=p(1-p) is a simple parabolic weighting closely related to entropy-based/uncertainty-based token reweighting; SRFT (Fu et al., 2025) already proposes a unified single-stage framework with sample-level SFT weighting, so the delta over prior work is primarily token-level rather than sample-level weighting.

There is little theoretical or principled justification for the specific form of ϕ(·); the 'information-theoretic' motivation (p(1-p) as uncertainty) is heuristic, and no theoretical analysis of the method's convergence or stability properties is provided.

Some reported gains are small and may be within evaluation variance: e.g., on BFCL, CHORD-ϕ (78.5) vs. Pure RL (77.1); no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported despite using avg@32/avg@8 to reduce variance. AIME has only 30 problems per year, so headline improvements like +1.0 on AIME24 are fragile.
Some results are internally inconsistent with the narrative: CHORD-μ notably underperforms SFT-best+RL on MMLU-Pro (43.3 vs 51.3), which is not well explained.

Baseline comparisons may be favorable to the proposed method: LUFFY is run with substantially fewer samples than its original configuration, and results are reported at the 'best checkpoint determined by the validation set', which can disadvantage methods evaluated differently or favor methods with more checkpoint selection.

The motivation is primarily empirical (a single model/expert pair for the 'shift-readapt-overfit' analysis); the generalization of this observation across models and data distributions is not systematically established.

Hyperparameter sensitivity of the μ schedule (start/end values, decay horizon) is acknowledged but not fully resolved, and the practical advantage of the full dual-control mechanism over simply using ϕ with a small fixed μ is not sharply quantified.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-organized empirical analysis of training dynamics when fine-tuning instruction-tuned models on off-policy expert data, identifying a 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression (Figures 1-2) that motivates the method
The proposed CHORD framework is simple, computationally cheap (only element-wise probability-based weighting), and easy to implement on top of standard GRPO pipelines

The experimental coverage is broad: two task domains (math reasoning and tool-use), multiple policy models (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, LLaMA3.2-3B, Phi-mini-MoE), multiple expert sources, non-verifiable domains (RaR-Medicine), and several relevant baselines (SFT-then-RL, LUFFY, SASR, SRFT, Pure RL)

Ablation studies are relatively thorough, including variants of the token-weighting function (entropy-based, clipping, focal loss), adaptive vs. decaying vs. fixed μ schedules, and joint μ/ϕ tuning (Appendix B)
The authors are candid about limitations (e.g., hyperparameter sensitivity of adaptive μ, the ϕ design being 'one instantiation of a general principle'), which is appreciated
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is a linear loss interpolation L = (1−μ)L_GRPO + μ·L_SFT with a decay schedule, which is essentially scheduled sampling / loss-level data mixing — ideas already present in interleaved SFT-RL methods, SRFT, and UFT. The token-wise weight ϕ(p) = p(1−p) is a simple uncertainty-based heuristic; entropy-based token selection (Wang et al., 2025) and importance-sampling-style SFT reweighting (DFT, iw-SFT) are closely related and cited only tangentially. The ablations in Table 4/5 show entropy-based variants perform comparably, which further undercuts the significance of the specific ϕ design

The central empirical claim rests largely on qualitative curve inspection. The 'shift-readapt-overfit' analysis (Figure 2) is based on a single model-dataset configuration with no repetition, variance estimates, or quantitative metrics (e.g., KL to expert, token-level disruption measures), weakening the 'systematic and in-depth analysis' claim in the contribution list

Evaluation fairness concerns: results are reported at the 'best checkpoint determined by the validation set' for all methods, which may disproportionately favor the proposed methods if their curves are more varied. The headline gains are modest (e.g., +1.0 on AIME24 over SFT-best+RL) and, despite avg@32, no standard deviations or significance tests are reported

Some inconsistencies weaken confidence: CHORD-µ uses a decay schedule while CHORD-ϕ uses a fixed μ, making the two variants hard to compare cleanly; the MMLU-Pro result for CHORD-µ (43.3) is worse than Pure RL (45.8) while CHORD-ϕ (56.2) is a large outlier (+10 over all baselines), which is under-explained

Theoretical grounding is thin. There is no gradient analysis or justification for why p(1−p) is the right weighting beyond informal information-theoretic intuition; the claim that down-weighting both probability extremes 'prevents disruption' and 'prevents entropy collapse' is asserted from correlating entropy-loss curves, not established

The distinction from prior work ('we tune instruct models, others tune base models') is a valid but narrow differentiator; much of the framing overstates the gap, and the comparison with SRFT/LUFFY (Table 12) uses a different (smaller) expert data budget, complicating attribution of the gains

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper unifies SFT and RL through an on-policy/off-policy lens and provides an instructive empirical analysis of the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression when applying off-policy expert data to instruction-tuned models (Figures 1-2), which is a practically important and underexplored setting (most prior work like LUFFY/SRFT targets base models in a 'zero-RL' regime).

The proposed dual-control mechanism is simple, computationally cheap, and well-justified: the global decaying coefficient µ handles the coarse off-policy-to-on-policy transition, while the token-wise weight ϕ(p)=p(1−p) addresses the entropy collapse (IS-style) vs. distribution disruption (unweighted SFT) dilemma with an interpretable instantiation, supported by entropy/reward dynamics analyses (Figures 5, 8-9).

Comprehensive and honest experimental evaluation: multiple tasks (math reasoning, tool-use, non-verifiable medical QA), multiple models (Qwen2.5-7B, LLaMA3.2-3B, weaker Qwen2.5-3B, Phi-mini-MoE), multiple expert sources, variance-reduced metrics (avg@32/avg@8), and comparisons against a broad set of recent baselines including LUFFY, SASR, and SRFT in the instruction-model setting (Appendix D.1).

Thoughtful ablations: variants of the weighting function (entropy-based, clipping, focal loss), adaptive vs. fixed µ schedules, and joint tuning of µ with ϕ; the authors candidly acknowledge that ϕ(·) is one instantiation of a general principle and that hyperparameter sensitivity remains.

Analysis beyond raw accuracy, including response length/pattern analysis (Tables 2, 6) and qualitative case studies, which substantiates the claim that CHORD selectively absorbs expert patterns rather than wholesale imitation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contributions are (i) a weighted sum of GRPO and SFT losses with a decaying coefficient, and (ii) a token-wise weight ϕ(p)=p(1−p). Both components have close precedents the paper itself cites (scheduled sampling; iw-SFT of Qin & Springenberg 2025; DFT; SRFT's sample-level weighting; high-entropy minority token findings of Wang et al. 2025). The delta over these concurrent/unified approaches is incremental, and the paper does not provide a direct experimental comparison against iw-SFT/DFT-style token-level SFT weighting in isolation.

The headline of 'dynamic weighting' is somewhat overstated for CHORD-ϕ, the strongest variant, which uses a fixed µ = 0.1; the genuinely dynamic component (µ decay) is shown to be non-essential once ϕ is applied (Appendix B.7), weakening the framing.

Magnitude of gains is modest and mixed on some benchmarks: e.g., on AIME24/AIME25 improvements over SFT-best+RL are ~1 point, and CHORD-µ clearly underperforms SFT-best+RL on MMLU-Pro (43.3 vs 51.3); no statistical significance tests are reported, and results appear to be from single training runs despite avg@k evaluation.

Potential baseline fairness concerns: the footnote admits LUFFY was run with substantially fewer SFT samples (500 vs. 5k) and 20k vs. 45k RL samples than its original setup; while the authors justify this, it leaves room for doubt about whether baselines were fully tuned, and 'best checkpoint on validation set' selection may favor methods with more checkpoint choices.

The theoretical grounding is thin: claims such as the 'learning sweet spot' and the information-theoretic interpretation of p(1−p) are heuristic; there is no analysis of when down-weighting both probability extremes is provably beneficial, and the general principle is validated only empirically on relatively small models (3B-7B) and limited data scales.

The 'shift-readapt-overfit' characterization, while well illustrated, is based on a single model-dataset pair and could be an artifact of aggressive learning rates; no investigation of how SFT hyperparameters (lr, epochs) modulate this progression.
